strings.VEN_selected_city_0_desc_key: Maracaibo is one of Venezuela's biggest prides, the oil city that built an empire of steel and smoke. The lake glitters with rigs and rust alike, its shores lined with refineries. The city's elites still clutch at what power remains, trading favors for barrels. Whoever holds Maracaibo holds the flow of fuel that keeps the nation alive.
strings.VEN_selected_city_1_desc_key: El Vigía lies nestled between mountains and plains, a humid crossroad of diesel and fog. Trucks move through its streets night and day, hauling supplies across the Andes. Its small airfield is a quiet lifeline, perfect for moving things that shouldn't be seen. This small but key trading hub is one of the arteries that feeds the west.
strings.VEN_selected_city_2_desc_key: Vega de Aza is a small, quiet town lost in the Andes, little more than a cluster of checkpoints and tired soldiers. Smugglers and travelers pass through, leaving behind rumors, gossip and cash. It's a place where everyone knows when to look away. Perhaps, this might be one of the western border's only reliable gates.
strings.VEN_selected_city_3_desc_key: The capital city of Táchira, San Cristóbal sits high atop the Andes, a city of trade, contraband, and restless talk. Colombian money flows through its markets, and its people through its streets. The cold air smells of fuel and politics, San Cristóbal may very well be a deciding factor whether the frontier stays open.
strings.VEN_selected_city_4_desc_key: Guasdualito stretches along the Venezuelan great plains, the Llanos, serving as a key passage between Venezuela and Colombia. Traders, soldiers, and mercenaries cross its bridges every day. The heat never lifts, and neither does the tension. Guasdualito is the roadway through which men and supplies could secure the eastern Llanos.
strings.VEN_selected_city_5_desc_key: Cabudares grows beside the Barquisimeto metro area, its factories humming with restless workers. Its streets young, growing fast, and filled with restless youth who march once the police look away. At the very heart of Lara, a perfect spark for urban unrest should the country tremble.
strings.VEN_selected_city_6_desc_key: San Carlos sits alone deep in the Llanos, quiet and steady beneath a blazing sun as the agricultural core and capital city of Cojedes, surrounded by fertile plains and old colonial estates. Convoys refuel here before vanishing into the horizon. As radios go silent, the logistical ghost town will surely keep the army fed.
strings.VEN_selected_city_7_desc_key: San Felipe rests in a valley characterized by its sugar plantations and silence, its fields swaying under a tired sun. The old landowners, families from colonial times, still whisper in the cafés, waiting to see which flag flies next. Whoever owns the capital city of Yaracuy secures the path to the capital.
strings.VEN_selected_city_8_desc_key: Puerto Cabello, still scarred by El Porteñazo a few years earlier, lives and dies by its port, a historical major gateway from Venezuela to the Caribbean and the rest of the world. Smugglers, foreign agents, and loyalists all dock here under the same tired cranes. Commanding its harbor means deciding what gets in, and who gets out.
strings.VEN_selected_city_9_desc_key: Maracay, an industrial and military hub west of Caracas, surrounded by lush valleys and hills. The factories work in shifts that never stop, churning out parts for machines of war. If a conspiracy is to succeed, it must first pass through the gateway to Caracas, among the officers who know which way the wind is blowing.
strings.VEN_selected_city_10_desc_key: Caracas, the City of Eternal Spring, rises like a mirage surrounded by the mountains, dense and feverish, alive at every hour. Politicians hide in glass towers gleaming above slums while the streets whisper of revolt. Power shifts here by the minute, never truly resting. All roads lead to Caracas, and they end at the palace gates.

strings.VEN_ESQ_desc:
After nearly a century of territorial disputes between Venezuela and the United Kingdom's colony of Guyana, Venezuela has finally invaded over the disputed Essequibo strip, a piece of land constituting two thirds of Guyana's territory and a fifth of their population. With Venezuela now under a fascist and so-called “Bolivarian” regime, the invasion was nothing but expected.

Still, it has caught both Guyanese and Canadian forces off-guard, and as a member of the OFN, allied forces are expected to back up the small Guyanese army. However with Essequibo's rural and remote location, the Guyanese will need to hold back their invaders and push them back to the border until the OFN arrives.
strings.VEN_VR_desc:
Our Venezuelan ally nearly fell to a massive offensive by the communist FALN, but maintained their hold with significant force. Now the rebels lick their wounds in the Andes, while mustering their adherents at their bastion of Ciudad Bolivar and traitors within hamlets and universities.

Another red wave is coming. We must break its crest, or lose Venezuela forever.

strings.VEN_Jovito_Villalba_hog_desc:
Minister of Internal Affairs
National Liberalism
--------------
To take a man of middling stature like Jóvito Villalba lightly would be to greatly mislead oneself. Though his well-mannered demeanor and weary appearance may incite visions of a civil servant or accountant more than a revolutionary, without Villalba, Venezuela would not breathe today. What an Amazonian soldier does with his rifle and spirit, Villalba has done with equal fervor through impassioned speeches and late nights of writing.

From his days as an idealistic student campaigning against Gómez to his stand against Pérez Jiménez, vigor and integrity remained core to Villalba's values. Though he would suffer for it, from jail to exile, he remained unbroken. In 1952, he would stand against Pérez Jiménez, defeating the dictator in a military election at the zenith of his influence. For the years following, an exiled Villalba would become the mouthpiece of resistance against the regime, lighting a match that would explode into a wildfire in 1958.

Larrazábal would see a kindred spirit in Villalba, stepping down from office to run alongside his newfound ally. A populist campaign of restoration would follow, in which Larrazábal would become its grinning public face, and Villalba its arms and legs.

Jóvito has built the government he was denied in 1952, with the trust of the people and faith in his government, hoping to usher in a wave in politics, one where his vision for URD and the country may come to fruition. Not just a party of hope, but one of national unity to bring together all of Venezuela's lost children and give them the torch to light their way forward.
strings.VEN_Alfredo_Tarre_Murzi_sec_desc:
Minister of Defense
Christian Progressivism
--------------
Writers and politicians usually come hand in hand, the frantic scurrying of ideas, the chaotic drumming of mental noise, the fuel of caffeine and alcohol, and the somber bliss of completion of said work. For Alfredo Tarre Murzi, this has made the marriage of the two in his career a perfect compliment.

When Tarre Murzi writes, he is a critic - ever at the typewriter, infallible and indomitable, and when he is a politician he is frugal, warm, and a keen negotiator. Such skills have made him an indispensable pick for Jóvito Villalba's cabinet; a man able to read the turning tides of the new decade of Venezuelan history built in the fallout of the Pérez Jiménez dictatorship.

Tarre Murzi has worked tirelessly to create a Venezuela of compromise, between the military, the police and the people. Though this has never been easy, riots plaguing the first two years of Larrazábal's presidency, and military dissidence remaining a core issue within the country, the forces that once were at one another's throats have settled their daggers at ease, at least for now.

As for Tarre Murzi, he remains the conciliator in all of this. Where lesser men may have perhaps bowed to one or the other, or cowed to both, he, with all the warmth an aging statesman can give, reminds the disparate of Venezuela they owe allegiance not to him, but to their country.
strings.VEN_Miguel_Angel_Burelli_for_desc:
Minister of Outer Affairs
Liberal Conservatism
--------------
In backrooms filled with the ashy air of cigar smoke, and sweaty men pouring over policy reports and documentation, hastily desperate to ensure their own horse wins in the proverbial constant race of politics, Miguel Burelli Rivas stands as a man at ease. The gristle of the underside of politics has long remained his forte, whether that be the schizophrenic world of foreign affairs or the nail-biting psychosis of economic policy - Burelli Rivas remains a careerist through and through.

Born to an Italian father, languages would come easily to the young Rivas, learning several before even leaving university in Madrid. A core internationalist, he traveled vast distances before being ushered under the wing of Jóvito Villalba, who quickly recognized a protégé within him. When traveling, his thick jowls, smoker's voice, and bulldogged persistence would soon win him comparisons to a young Republican front-runner, to mixed reactions from Burelli himself.

Going forward, Burelli has placed his trust in Villalba - Venezuela needs leadership above all else, politics aside. After the decade his country has seen, all Burelli seeks is competence, from whom and where, irrespective.

Good politics require good men.
strings.VEN_Fabricio_Ojeda_eco_desc:
Economic Minister
Revolutionary Gaitanismo
--------------
Amongst the heroes of the 1958 Venezuelan Revolution, the downtrodden and lost Venezuelan society sings only one man's name from the bell towers to the slums.

Fabricio Ojeda, one of Venezuela's youngest politicians at only seventeen, became a pillar of the emerging Unión Republicana Democrática. Hopes of a republican society, truly free of the ties that had bound it, were scattered to the wind, however - Venezuelan democracy, like its founder, Rómulo Betancourt, would perish on a cold January morning.

In the hushed society built by Pérez Jiménez, his lofty ambitions would crush those on society's lower rungs like ants. Ojeda would stand in open defiance with the people of his birthplace. Though Larrazábal may have led the Revolution, without Ojeda's rallying call or communications across all of Venezuelan society, no coup would have ever been possible.

In the post-war government, Ojeda had won Larrazábal's trust as an apt Economic Minister. In a few short years, the boot of Perezjimenismo had been lifted from the people's necks. In Ojeda's deepest wishes, however, the boots that once wished to crush them would soon be on the feet of every man and woman in the barrios - not just to walk towards a brighter future, but to dare to run to it.
strings.VEN_black_gold_raw_gold_desc: As Italy's lifeblood flows like wine, and Russia's like Vodka, Venezuela's flows like oil, twice as thick and double as strong. The Venezuelan economy, since the nation's inception, has been one built on the banks of the Orinoco River, and the belt which runs throughout it. Such a boon has won her a special candor with the other nations of the Organization of Free Nations. Though Venezuela may, in a season of plenty, cultivate a great harvest, she has grown too comfortable from a long spring - one which may soon turn to fall.
strings.VEN_black_gold_raw_gold_alt_desc:
As Italy's lifeblood flows like wine, and Russia's like Vodka, Venezuela's flows like oil, twice as thick and double as strong. The Venezuelan economy, since the nation's inception, has been one built on the banks of the Orinoco River, and the belt which runs throughout it. Such a boon has won her a special candor with the other nations of Latin America. Though Venezuela may, in a season of plenty, cultivate a great harvest, she has grown too comfortable from a long spring - one which may soon turn to fall.

And now, with the establishment of the new regime, the King of Oil opens the gates of its palace to new, foreign visitors. No longer do the Bald Eagle and Golden Eagle feast on Venezuela's oil reserves, monopolizing the riches like a prey, as investors from the Old World have begun flooding the country's market. Unbound to the chains that formerly kept her tied to Mexican and American interests, Venezuela stands now as the master of her own destiny.
strings.VEN_game_of_the_three_kings_desc:
The fall of one tyrant, as it tends to do, leaves his kingdom shattered and its people lost - shattered between fiefdoms. Since the fall of Pérez Jiménez, and the death of national hero Rómulo Betancourt, three giants have been stuck in perpetual competition: AD, led by Raúl Leoni, COPEI, led by Rafael Caldera, and URD, led by Jóvito Villalba, have been locked in a bitter political rivalry over the nation's future.

Though in 1958 that unease may have been sufficed by the election of the people's admiral, Wolfgang Larrazábal, the hero of the 1958 Coup, as the next elections approach, so does factionalism - and the ghosts of past enmity.
strings.VEN_game_of_the_three_kings_barrios_desc:
The fall of one tyrant, as it tends to do, leaves his kingdom shattered and its people lost - shattered between fiefdoms. Since the fall of Pérez Jiménez, and the death of national hero Rómulo Betancourt, three giants have been stuck in perpetual competition: AD, led by Gonzalo Barrios, COPEI, led by Rafael Caldera, and URD, led by Jóvito Villalba, have been locked in a bitter political rivalry over the nation's future.

Though in 1958 that unease may have been sufficed by the election of the people's admiral, Wolfgang Larrazábal, the hero of the 1958 Coup, as the next elections approach, so does factionalism - and the ghosts of past enmity.
strings.VEN_game_of_the_three_kings_prieto_desc:
The fall of one tyrant, as it tends to do, leaves his kingdom shattered and its people lost - shattered between fiefdoms. Since the fall of Pérez Jiménez, and the death of national hero Rómulo Betancourt, three giants have been stuck in perpetual competition: AD, led by Luis Beltrán Prieto Figueroa, COPEI, led by Rafael Caldera, and URD, led by Jóvito Villalba, have been locked in a bitter political rivalry over the nation's future.

Though in 1958 that unease may have been sufficed by the election of the people's admiral, Wolfgang Larrazábal, the hero of the 1958 Coup, as the next elections approach, so does factionalism - and the ghosts of past enmity.
strings.VEN_democracys_fraying_lifeline_desc:
With the fall of Marcos Pérez Jiménez, so was felled 150 years of Venezuelan militarism, and the brief experiment of Venezuelan democracy, launched by Betancourt and Gallegos in 1945, was vindicated. Those in the military, however, shaped to rule by previous military regimes, rest uneasy with this break from tradition, from the high offices to the lowly academies.

Ideas, new and old, are fostered in the name of Venezuela, above democracy or dictatorship, and should the military believe its interests are jeopardized, dissident forces will do anything possible to save the Republic.

In the rural landscapes and mountains, a lowly song plays - half of tragedy for a past lost, half of hope. In 1958, these people were nearly vindicated, and yet their hope, under the watchful eye of right-wing traitors and the American eagle, stole a truly free Venezuela from them.

Now, under the guise of another generation of revolutionaries, the MIR and PCV have united under the burgeoning FALN's banner and taken up arms. From the tropics of Zulia to the plains of Bolívar a slow hum plays, ever present but low - however, as Venezuela enters her most uncertain decade to date, what is a hum may turn to a shout, to a scream, to a cry for all the country to hear.

strings.VEN_el_esequibo_es_nuestro_desc:
“First stolen by the Anglos, then by the Yankees.”

Though the fires of nationalism were tempered with the Guyanese and Venezuelan alliance under the OFN, there is no hiding the ruse of land that cannot be held. For now, the Venezuelan matriarchal anger may be calmed, but only on the comfort of their lost sons and daughters across the border - and should that change, so will the wrath of the mother.
strings.VEN_One_Under_Bandera_desc:
The path to revolution as it was in Russia, as it was in Cuba, is never the bright, blinding flash that the revolutionary mind may idealise. The petty feuding, squabbling, and bickering, although callous and hollow, eventually gives way against all its doubters.

The Democratic Republican Union has fulfilled its destiny even in the wake of its greatest detractors. The revolution sparked first in the fifties has now, against all the forces that sought to weaken it, been vindicated by unrelenting success.

Left unopposable and unapologetic, Venezuela has chosen its fate, one that lies solely in the hands of its most principled revolutionaries.
strings.VEN_vanguards_of_the_flag_desc:
Men who serve pledge their life to an ideal rather than a state, that of servitude and loyalty to a nation. Such ideals embolden men to choose, above all, the good of the nation above all. This is what it means to be a soldier of Venezuela, to be bound to this brutality of reality and its hard decisions.

Henceforth, Venezuela has been taken into the hands of men rigid in such beliefs and, with it, who know their duty is to lead their nation when it has lost its way.

Against those of the street who call them monsters, butchers, the children who hurl fruit at them. They know what they do is right.
strings.VEN_the_brightest_and_boldest_desc:
Ideals born in the impassioned university halls, boardrooms and smoke-fueled backrooms, governed by cigars and imported school alumni, unexpectedly rule the nation they spoke of in such high spirits.

The transitional government of Eugenio Mendoza's defining characteristic was to be run by intellectuals and scholars rather than politicians, those chosen by mind rather than votes, such high ideals have invoked a nation of gathering hope. Yet with the hope of ambition comes recklessness, such that will only become tested with the turning of time, and the brutality of reality that come with it.
strings.VEN_the_jewel_of_the_caribbean_desc:
Against the fraying tethers of division that enraptured her, Venezuela has seen through its most tumultuous decade and, with it, been rewarded with countless fortunes. Its once burdensome factionalism and the oil that threatened to drench her have become the lifeline to which she has become the darling of the Americas.

What the future will bring for the ever-young democracy is still to be seen, though she has shaken off the ghosts of the last decade and emerged unshackled and, in such a way, allowed something to blossom that has been long lost in her history.

Hope, and the joys that come with it.
strings.VEN_Venezuela_Reborn_desc:
Like the Phoenix, the ill-begotten spirit of democracy shall be reinvigorated in Venezuela, not by the sword, but by the pen and the slow and tumultuous efforts of Eugenio Mendoza and his disciples. This democracy as of the nation it serves, however, is being transformed into a being wholly anew.

Shackled by the visions of intellectuals and magnates, this new democracy is one fueled by progress and pragmatism. The once bright-eyed populism that governed it dead, now divided by the funding ideals of new monarchs, the burgeoning middle class and all of their flaws.

For this time, let us hope it will hold.
strings.VEN_the_quiet_revolution_desc:
The drum that beats to herald change is rarely noticed by even by the common man - the raucous of the streets, chattering of politicians and steam of industry too caught up to notice the quiet echo, until it becomes deafening. The Democratic Republican Union, the party that felled a dictator, have served as the stick of which those drums were beaten to for now over a decade which now deafen the nation itself.

From the spirited Fabricio Ojeda, to the charming Alirio Ugarte Pelayo, the fathers of this revolution have not issued change from the barrel of a gun, but rather the slow methodical reformation of a state from its very inception. Born in the spark of revolution, Venezuela's is finally complete.
strings.VEN_charter_of_the_masses_desc:
The cries of mud-slinging peasants, of soot-covered industry men, of working girls and boys from the street have been the song of history - ever trodden into the foot beneath the feet of their betters. Now, unlike ever before, their forlorn cry has been heard, and reciprocated with the rage of a nation in anguish.

Caudillos, Adecos, Copeyanos, Urredistas - they all now lie to the wasteside. In their place, a charter drawn against a great red banner - a people under a party indivisible against itself, bound by the humility of the common man and against the tyranny of the bourgeois that have so long haunted it.
strings.VEN_along_the_shores: Along The Shores of the Orinoco
strings.VEN_along_the_shores_desc:
In a matter of months, the world split in seems and, suddenly, the man's grip on his gun in Arabia starved the suburbanite in Chicago. For most of the world, they went mad as the engine of their lifestyles was put on auction and thousands wrestled for a taste of such sickly black ooze.

In Venezuela, the sound of bursting champagne is far louder than the rest of the world's bickering. The nation, ever rich, has found itself engulfed in a period of unfathomable economic growth as barrel after barrel, dollar after dollar, changes hands. Venezuela has entered the new decade not to the sound of gunsmoke, bullets or wailing - but to the sound of rapturous laughter.
strings.VEN_Port_of_Spain_desc:
Two fencers lay down their sabres after a century-long session. Though neither has truly won out, and hot-headed rivalry still takes precedence over sound mind and body, for now the Essequibo River stands quiet - its bubbling streams and rivers left only to nature instead of the beating drums of war.

Designed by Rafael Caldera, the Port of Spain Treaty guarantees the collaboration between both Venezuela and Guyana, as well as their Canadian overlords, over continued peace in the region. Though only a twelve-year memorandum, the Treaty has done much to simmer the bubbling heat between the two nations over the banks of the Essequibo River.
strings.VEN_Port_of_Spain_HMMLR_desc:
Two fencers lay down their sabres after a century-long session. Though neither has truly won out, and hot-headed rivalry still takes precedence over sound mind and body, for now the Essequibo River stands quiet - its bubbling streams and rivers left only to nature instead of the beating drums of war.

Designed by Rafael Caldera, the Port of Spain Treaty guarantees the collaboration between both Venezuela and Guyana, as well as their British overlords, over continued peace in the region. Though only a twelve-year memorandum, the Treaty has done much to simmer the bubbling heat between the two nations over the banks of the Essequibo River.
strings.VEN_the_invisible_hand_desc:
Some philosophies do not die, even as the centuries past the theories of a Scotsman hold firm the puppet strings of the international order. Venezuela, a nation once governed by the fiery will of the masses, now sees its strings tugged by a far more unfeeling master.

Bound by its new constitution, the powers that be in Venezuela are now bound by its upper echelons, its oligarchs and magnates, a system broken on graphs and reports, and with it the dazzling rays of limitless development.
strings.VEN_drowned_in_pitch_black_desc:
The rich, black veins of Venezuela have been slashed through. Once plentifully flooding, its arteries have stopped. In doing, so the ire of the vampires which lap at her exposed nerves have been sent into a rage - the eagle, the bull and the adler. In the glory of the Bolivarian Revolution, the colonial forces and their puppets which have so long bled her dry have been repelled, and in doing so returned Venezuela's lifeblood unto her, for her to control as she wishes.

The once neverending waterfalls of oil to the Americas has been damned, and it is left to its Bolivarian masters whom has won the honour to drink from her again.
strings.VEN_bolivar_anew_desc:
The folly of weak men has led to this.

In their vanity, petulant bickering, weak wristed rule and blatant corruption, the blood of Venezuela has been shed - and to its scent, the wolves have descended. Emboldened by the spirit of their long lost forefather, Simón Bolívar, the flag of the Fourth Republic has been torn down, and old spirits and animosity have begun to feast on her corpse.

And now, the Bolivarian Republic stands anew, drenched in the blood of her forefather.
strings.VEN_the_young_bolivar_desc:
Often, it is the folly of the revolutionary to never learn from history. Drunk with the vigour of change, they are left open to the passions they themselves ignited and are butchered from inside - rather than out.

Such was the fate of the Bolivarian Revolution, once an ideological symphony of nationalist xenophobia, the movement and icons of its principles have been remolded and refitted. Emerged from it are the renewed principles of the new, young Bolívar, and his erstwhile disciples.

A socialist republic, entrenched into immortality by the strong hand of her most erstwhile patriots - the unbreakable Bolivarian Armed Forces.
strings.VEN_all_roads_led_to_rome_desc:
One king fell to the pitchforks of his angered peasants, another to the heresy of his kin and the last crushed beneath the weight of the crown he attempted to wear. In their squabbling, the petty feudals would fail to hear the sound of the drums long echoing, until, of course, it became deafening - The victory march of not kings, but emperors.

Marcos Pérez Jiménez is not a symptom, nor a cause, he became an inevitability. A nation, carved solely in his image and finely tailored over the years to his suiting. For him, and indeed for Venezuela, his return marks a merge of nation and leader into one as once again Caesar seizes his long lost crown.
strings.VEN_all_roads_led_to_rome_margot_desc:
One king fell to the pitchforks of his angered peasants, another to the heresy of his kin and the last crushed beneath the weight of the crown he attempted to wear. In their squabbling, the petty feudals would fail to hear the sound of the drums long echoing, until, of course, it became deafening - The victory march of not kings, but emperors.

Marcos Pérez Jiménez was not a symptom, nor a cause, he became an inevitability. A nation, carved solely in his image and finely tailored over the years to his suiting. For him, and indeed for Venezuela, his return marked a merge of nation and leader into one as once again Caesar seized his long lost crown.

But the end of this tragedy came unexpectedly. In a moment of weakness, the court tore apart the monarch's rotting corpse, and, almost ironically, the heir to the throne ascended, now trapped within the ivory tower in her gilded cage and her own decay.
strings.VEN_sins_of_history_desc:
Hatred was the gravedigger of what Venezuela became. In the squabbles of division, the once smouldering torch of democratic hope was extinguished, and those who used it to guide their way were torn apart by the wolves.

The Bolivarian regime has left a long, unmistakable gash across the heart of the nation, thousands left flung in hasty graves, families shattered, a people divided, a war fought as much in the minds of its people as it was in the fields of war.

In the decades to come she will heal. For now, leave her to weep.
strings.VEN_sins_of_history2_desc:
Hatred was the gravedigger of what Venezuela became. In the squabbles of division, the once smouldering torch of democratic hope was extinguished, and those who used it to guide their way were torn apart by the wolves.

The Bolivarian regime has left a long, unmistakable gash across the heart of the nation, thousands left flung in hasty graves, families shattered, a people divided, a war fought as much in the minds of its people as it was in the fields of war.

In the decades to come she will heal. For now, leave her to weep.
strings.VEN_to_aspire_to_better_desc:
The wounds torn bloody by the dogs of Bolívar will take decades to heal. The death of Venezuela's fertile democracy's still leaves many hopeless and, for now, the scrabble for its future remains vague and aimless. Many, left with no hopes in the crippled nation, have taken to its shores, leaving the ill-begotten nation behind.

But those left have begun the slow efforts of reconstruction to a nation many see as hopeless. Enrique Tejera París, though regarded by many as a mere gringo puppet, through close cooperation with the OFN and OAS, has taken upon himself the responsibility and burden of the guardianship of his country to care for, represent and administer his people. As the years to follow will show, time heals all wounds.
strings.VEN_gringos_fuera_desc:
“Yankee, go home” they sing as the foreign riflemen watch them from the rooftops - the same men pelleted by stones from wayward children, and spat on by woeful grandmothers. The memory of the Americano is fleeting, but for the Venezuelan, unending such is the woe that has begotten their country.

Those most taken by their anguish turn to the slums and mountains once more, sequestered into invisible armies for such men the war never ended, never faltered and they fight on, whether that be a soldier vanished into the night, or the cities set alight by the smoulder of napalm.
strings.VEN_outside_the_enclosure_desc:
Day after day, hour after hour, the diplomats scurry back and forth from the bruised walls of the half-destroyed Miraflores Palace. Reports, proposals, rebuttals, plans, graphs and charts, endless as they are bleak - Yet to process a nation's woe is little to experience it.

A small stretch from the palace, you will find a nation embittered by division in the rural landscapes. Burnt plainslands, scourged rainforests, communities slaughtered. Much is to be done, but for now, Miraflores counts its cards and does the little it can.
strings.VEN_civilization_and_barbarism_desc:
Truly, as they say, reality often beats fiction. As the late former President Rómulo Gallegos wrote in his novel 'Doña Bárbara', “Progress will penetrate the plain, and barbarism will retreat, defeated.”

Outstretched along the vast plains of this nation is the grand opportunity for life uncurtailed, of hope and family, and yet now all she speaks is that of atrocious death. Those who watched their land turn to the barbarism of the last decade may only blame themselves, the vindication of history does little to subsume guilt.

In such, they live a life to bring some small redemption to brutality, to redeem great ideas and great men and to rebuild a civilisation that once lit the fires of democracy in the continent.

Never will be it be easy, but they have their lives to do it.
--------------
“You're wrong, Santos, the times of barbarism haven't passed; I am barbarism, and I'm still here. There's still plenty of Doña Bárbara to go around.”
strings.VEN_peacekeeping_force_desc:
We gathered on the shorelines to watch them, our cerulean liberators who emerged from their boats to raucous applause. They stood back to back with our community leaders, our kinsmen and exiles, they rode into towns with no hope like some azurean knights from a fairytale.

In the Venezuela left by the Bolivarians, they at first seemed like salvation, an end to horror of the last few years, and when my son rode on the shoulders of some young corporal I could almost forget...
strings.VEN_or_an_unwanted_presence_desc:
...what I saw them do in the streets of our cities, their drunken hands in the bars, the women left ashamed, fooled into dreams of escape, hands bloodied with those of our sons, their callous mockery, their careless orders.

One master was traded for another, as we have forsaken Bolívar, we have let Uncle Sam in, a man not so forgiving to our ways, one ready to trample our culture and people into the dirt, to leave a stamp where democracy used to tread.
strings.VEN_democracys_decimated_corpse_desc:
It tried, in all that it could, to uplift the spirits of men, to build a nation on the foundations of hope, the spirits of freedoms and the optimism of a new decade. That is all that can be said for a dream dead in its cradle, torn asunder by infighting, stark division and the vultures of nationalism - such demons taunted the young democracy into a shallow grave and scattered the visionaries which laid her.

Now, under the watchful grip of the zealotry of her military protectors, she has been returned to the immortal cycle of nationalism that has defined her history. They say it is for Bolívar, for the good of her people, yet in the eyes of the lowest infantryman, the grim truth is irrefutable.
strings.VEN_caesars_gambit_desc:
History will reflect that it is not with the dread of the marching boots Venezuelan democracy rotted, nor with the death rattle of a people crushed, but rather the flashing of cameras, the scurrying of the middle classes to get a better view, and the almost mocking grin of her new dictator, one vindicated by the failings of democracy and emboldened by a nation's short memory.

The democratic revolution will not be remembered fondly, Venezuela's new Caesar will be sure of that. Its failings are obvious to all who look up to see, towering above all, the statuesque figure of Perezjimenismo. Carved in marble by the complacency of its people, under it a pedestal reads.

“I am Ozymandias, King of Kings, Look Upon My Works Ye Mighty and Despair”
strings.VEN_eagles_in_the_sky_desc:
Time is a fickle mistress, ever the strumpet she does not lay down for men of ambition, nor that of good intentions.

Regularly, the men to take her eye are those who herald the unexpected, such bachelors bring visions of change and new horizons, her favourite boon indeed.

So, Venezuela changes from a nation of meritocracy and democracy to one of commerce and wealth, as she sways to the sweet tune of fortune, a song in which she will make many new bedfellows, from the bureaucrat in Madrid, to the officer in Berlin, to the statesman in Washington.

The bald eagle, schwarzer adler and águila imperial circle the skies, watching for the movement of their prey below - in a competition where the one that dies of hunger, loses.
strings.VEN_thrown_to_wolves_desc:
Almost three decades ago, three friends met with the shared spirit of a dream. One died by the assassin's bullet, one was consumed by the wolves he so sought to keep from the doors of his home, and the last was left confined to a small office in Mexico City. That Venezuela is dead, its flag chewed and torn as its wolves turn against those it once served to protect.

Yet in the face of hopelessness, a destiny once denied is flung open, left to the elements of a great storm.

Many will question its inevitability, the slowly burning match of revolution lit first in the 1920s under the Gomecista dictatorship left to scorch down to the nation's fingertips. Others will blame the scions of the state, grown bloated and fat with the nation's black blood and earthly temptations.

Little of what the historians say will bring much peace to the men who now draw arms, of the brother who turns against brother, sister against sister, as the nation finds itself in the flings of civil war. Whether men stand by the red flag or the tricolor, all that is clear is... that they are all true Venezuelans.

Decades of silencing, oppression and polarity led to the red tide that is sweeping Venezuela, the men once martyrs rise as magnates and the nation now hums to a new tune: the everlasting song of the internationale.
