strings.VEN_faln_state_modifier_desc:
Frontlines are often nothing more than lines on a map the jungle refuses to recognize. The Fuerzas Armadas de Liberación Nacional have turned the landscape itself into a complex network of partisan cells. To our soldiers, the war is no longer a matter of simple tactical maneuvers, but a marathon of paranoia.

Many locals within this state do not look at us with hope, but with a hollow, watchful resentment. We are, to them, merely an ecosystem waiting to be dismantled. Every step forward is a struggle - marching through sabotaged trails, fighting against constant ambushes, and realizing we are not conquering territory.

We are trespassing into a graveyard.
strings.VEN_ucmb_state_modifier_desc:
Operating with the legitimacy of a militia and the brutality of a death squad, the Unión Cívico-Militar Bolivariana's paramilitaries cling like parasites to the Venezuelan heartland, fighting to ensure there is nothing left for their enemies to inherit. Shadows around the corner, smoke on the horizon.

Their scorched-earth tactics are not merely strategic. They leave behind villages of ash and cities of whispers, using terror as a force multiplier to paralyze any thought of dissent. These bandit soldiers are loyal only to the survival of the regime and the spoils of war.

This state has traded its soul, and it is the civilian population that must bleed to keep its blade sharp.
strings.VEN_falncvw_state_modifier_desc:
Once a flickering ember of resistance has been forged into a cauterizing iron. The Fuerzas Armadas de Liberación Nacional - Bandera Roja did not just survive the Bolivarian extermination campaigns, they were hardened by them. No longer are they the idealistic students of the past, but the jaded remnants who decided that mercy was a luxury that their enemies did not deserve.

Their brand of Amazonist Marxism is a synthesis executed with a fanatical precision. They don't raid depots, they liquidate them. They don't harass patrols, they erase them.

In these regions, the red flag waved against the wind and has become a warning that the war has entered its most desperate, uncompromising phase.
strings.VEN_Puntofijo_Pact_desc:
Ever since the collapse of the Jiménez government in a coup and its replacement by a democratic polity, various measures were taken in order to ensure that Venezuelan democracy would never again fall apart in the face of tyranny. The Puntofijo Pact was the crystallisation of these plans; it was a written guarantee that the signatory parties would respect election results, prevent single-party hegemony, and work together to fight dictatorship.

However, all good things must come to an end, and that end seems to be coming rather quickly for the Puntofijo Pact. The once ironclad agreement is beginning to show cracks, and whether that will lead to its renewal or to its ruination no one can tell with certainty.
strings.VEN_Essequibo_Dispute_desc:
Guayana Essequibo is to Venezuela what the east is to Bolivia and the Falklands are to Argentina. As is the case with all such disputed territories in Latin America, it is a land forever claimed by its neighbour and a perennial problem for the people of the region.

Any and all Venezuelan politicians elected to any office above that of environmental health officer (that is, rat-catcher) breathes fire when asked about the region; they all aim to reclaim it, and that desire has brought even socialists and conservative hardliners together even if only for a few moments.

Obviously, if this is not controlled or solved in a rational manner, the Organisation of Free Nations—to which both Venezuela and Guyana currently belong—is at risk of being split over this.
strings.VEN_King_of_Oil_desc:
Verily, Venezuela is the King of Oil, and we are doing remarkably well with this position. The economy is doing marvellously, and since previous governments successfully nationalised it all we have total control over it. Yes, you heard it correctly: it's ours, all ours.

Our control over this large oil reserve enables us to punch well above our theoretical diplomatic weight. We can make friends and enemies as we please and suffer less than, say, the Colombians might if they copied our actions—all thanks to our oil.
strings.VEN_news.1.desc:
Grave news emerges from Venezuela today as a standoff in the city of Puerto Cabello has spilt blood over the city's streets, with many calling this one of the bloodiest government responses since the last days of Pérez Jiménez. The latest in a long line of insurrections, a collection of communist military dissidents, under the command of Officer Manuel Ponte Rodríguez, attempted to seize the city. A period of brutal fighting between the revolting officers and Armed Forces has left the city strewn with the bodies of the dead, and the rebellion ultimately failed.

The supposed aim of the revolt has been left up in the air, however, it seems much of the blame has landed on the Venezuelan Communist Party, which has experienced a sea of arrests, investigations and tribunals over the last few days, which has only increased public support for the communist movement.
strings.VEN_news.1.a: To give your all and be condemned for it is the leader's curse.
strings.VEN_news.1.b: The eagle is quick to pick off the mice that scurry near her nest.
strings.VEN_news.1.c: And so, the policy of reconciliation ends.
strings.VEN_news.2.desc:
The June 2nd Movement, which had staged an armed uprising in Puerto Cabello, has unexpectedly peacefully surrendered to the Venezuelan military. Fostered by Minister of Finance Fabricio Ojeda, a roundtable was held between Captain Manuel Ponte Rodríguez and President Larrazábal, who agreed on terms for the surrender.

The peace represents a breaking point in the hostility that has emerged between the Venezuelan government and its former partners in the socialist and communist left. This approach, however, has sparked hope for many of a peaceful future and calm collaboration moving forward. Rodríguez will face charges for the revolt, but he urged his followers to lay down their weapons peacefully. Although peace has returned to the city, the communist movement resumes in the interior of the country.
strings.VEN_news.2.a: A bone is thrown to the wolves.
strings.VEN_news.2.b: More to the man than his smiles would tell you.
strings.VEN_news.2.c: A tactful show of resolve in a dangerous interregnum?
strings.VEN_news.3.desc:
The meritocratic traditions of Venezuela have won out once again in the battle for the Presidency as Jóvito Villalba, the helmsman of the ruling party, and leading democratic advocate over the last decade, has won the recent presidential elections. Many initially expected Villalba to have taken this office years earlier, in the fallout of the Pérez Jiménez dictatorship after a long career fighting for a democratic transition.

However, his years serving as party chairman seem to have paid off, with Villalba viewed as the respectable, calm and stable individual in the cabinet amidst the chaos. Villalba has assured the Venezuelan public of his commitment to both peace and democracy, promising the gradual building of bulwarks to ensure a repeat of the military dictatorship remains impossible.
strings.VEN_news.3.b: Pérez Jiménez's shadow lifted step by step.
strings.VEN_news.3.c: A most warm friendship over the Caribbean.
strings.VEN_news.4.desc:
Fabricio Ojeda, Minister of Finance under the previous Larrazábal administration, has led a starkly different Democratic Republican Union to another victory. With a nail-bitingly close leadership election against chairman Jóvito Villalba, Ojeda secured a major upset over the URD's party establishment, and then used firebrand rhetoric to rouse the nation's masses in the recent 1963 Venezuelan elections.

From the raucous streets of the slums to the babbling party headquarters of the URD, Venezuelans once again chose change above all else. Ojeda's message of peace, transparency and equal opportunity held broad appeal - though some, particularly in the armed forces, have called the election a fluke and a dangerous uncertainty.

While Ojeda's supporters hope the need for peace will sheathe foes' daggers, few know for sure if this regime will last.
strings.VEN_news.4.a: A break in America's personal oil field.
strings.VEN_news.4.b: Such is the doom of socialism in South America.
strings.VEN_news.5.desc:
The progressive wave sweeping Latin America in the aftermath of Puerto Plata has finally reached Venezuela, as Gonzalo Barrios assumes the presidency. The political protégé of the late Rómulo Betancourt, Barrios never ceased his indignant attacks against fascism in the Americas after his mentor's death, a position now vindicated by the downfall of Rafael Trujillo.

After a hard-fought battle against Raúl Leoni for leadership of the Democratic Action party, Barrios managed to win the Presidency against all odds. With his reputation as a level headed and calm statesman, Barrios has promised a renewed fight for prosperity, education and equality. More than all, however, he has declared that fascism will have no home in Venezuela, and indeed in Latin America.
strings.VEN_news.5.a: A fool in shoes far too big for him.
strings.VEN_news.5.b: The torch never stopped burning in Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.5.c: An under-appreciated man from a gentler time.
strings.VEN_news.6.desc:
One of the founders of Venezuelan democracy, Raúl Leoni has been swept into the Presidency today on a monumental return of Democratic Action. The legacy of Rómulo Betancourt, the architect of not just AD, but of modern Venezuelan history, has today been vindicated in such a victory.

To some, it was a simple inevitable return of the old status quo, to others, following Leoni's sinking defeat in 1958, it seemed almost miraculous. Regardless, Leoni's past promises of stability, economic reliability and democratic virtues have remained his guiding objective. Already, the President has promised increased opportunities for Venezuelans, including the beginning of a battle against crime, terrorism and extremism, wherever it may be found, as Leoni begins to lay out his future plans for the development and stable growth of the nation.
strings.VEN_news.6.a: A firm hand from a weak man.
strings.VEN_news.6.b: Trujillo's great ploy has failed entirely.
strings.VEN_news.6.c: In the company of good friends.
strings.VEN_news.7.desc:
Reports arrive from Venezuela that Rafael Caldera, the renowned silver-tongued orator, has won the 1963 presidential election. From paperboys hawking headlines on the streets of Caracas to lively chatter, the legendary politician's victory has stirred the populace. Renowned for his eloquent speeches upholding moral leadership, Caldera stood out as a calming voice of unity amid division.

Caldera has laid out an ambitious vision to deliver long-awaited reforms. He promised to empower rural communities, strengthen worker protections, and safeguard religious freedoms for all. Most significantly, Caldera has vowed to reach a compromise with Guyana over the Essequibo dispute, much to the dismay of Venezuelan nationalists.

However, as COPEI gears up to lead the country into a bold new era of progress and prosperity, many feel Venezuela's best days are yet to come.
strings.VEN_news.7.a: The oil reserves are further distanced from us.
strings.VEN_news.7.b: Seems sanity has returned to Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.7.c: The sharpest tongue in Venezuela has out-waggled all others.
strings.VEN_news.8.desc:
Alarming news from Venezuela today, as once again the Armed Forces have seized power. The coup plotters, led by General Félix Román Moreno, stormed the Presidential Palace and arrested sitting President Jóvito Villalba, quickly displacing the civilian government. Many observers claim that Villalba's failure to properly pacify the armed forces and de-politicize the organization led to their sudden revolt.

General Róman Moreno, an ex-confidant of former dictator Marcos Pérez Jiménez and a leading figure among his supporters, has taken charge of the country. Promising that the new junta will only be temporary, the General claims the country needs a “grand restructuring” of the current constitution. For now, it seems Venezuela has not escaped the shadow of military strongmen.
strings.VEN_news.8.a: The ever-unquenchable fury of the Armed Forces.
strings.VEN_news.8.b: Venezuelan democracy never stood a chance.
strings.VEN_news.8.c: Pérez Jiménez's meddling will come back to bite him, sooner than he may think.
strings.VEN_news.9.desc:
From Ayacucho Hall, Venezuelan president Jóvito Villalba has announced a series of reforms to depoliticize the nation's military and subordinate it fully to civilian authority. While Villalba had previously been working with experts and his URD party on similar restrictions, their scale, scope, and likelihood of passage grew immensely overnight following a failed coup by military followers of the former dictator Pérez Jiménez.

Venezuelan intelligence and their Veracruz Pact allies were able to infiltrate the plot, allowing loyalist forces to bloodlessly capture the rebels as they attempted a midnight putsch. With senior military figures like Generals Félix Román Moreno implicated, Congress is expected to pass Villalba's reform agenda swiftly.
strings.VEN_news.9.a: A long night, but few knives for Villalba.
strings.VEN_news.45.desc:
A tense and divisive day in Venezuela today as the government in Caracas has agreed to a temporary suspension of the nations's democratic institutions. With the current stalling on the frontlines, many within the military have pressured government officials to resign in what is being considered a bloodless coup.

A temporary military junta has been formed, led by Pablo Antonio Florez Álvarez, a well-respected General renown for his efforts to restore apoliticism and respect to the previously divided and radical Armed Forces. While protests have broken out in major urban areas, with many feeling apprehensive about signing away democratic power to the military once more, they have been met with a brutal crackdown, much to the dismay of Venezuela's allies inside the Veracruz Pact and OFN.
strings.VEN_news.45.a: The last scream of a dying nation.
strings.VEN_news.45.b: A bold choice considering her history of military rule.
strings.VEN_news.45.c: A necessary measure, a temporary setback...
strings.VEN_news.11.desc:
Only six years after the last military coup in Venezuela, another has been launched today under the leadership of General Jesús María Castro León. Castro León, a prominent figure in the regime of former dictator Marcos Pérez Jiménez, has long been outraged by the return of the so-called “institutionally corrupt” Democratic Action and has sought their removal.

After seizing control of telecommunication and radio stations, the military was able to capture the Palace of Miraflores. Castro León has publicly promised to eliminate subversive elements within Venezuela by establishing a temporary junta to enact his “5 National Points”, a proposed reorganization of the nation's constitution. While the military and the oligarchs firmly support Castro León, many Venezuelans are uncertain about the end goal of his “reorganization.”
strings.VEN_news.11.c: A dangerous individual of unknown quantity.
strings.VEN_news.12.desc:
Only six years after the last military coup in Venezuela, another has been launched today under the leadership of General Jesús María Castro León. Castro León, a prominent figure in the regime of former dictator Marcos Pérez Jiménez, launched the coup in response to the election of Fabricio Ojeda, a Cuban Revolution-inspired socialist, as President.

After seizing control of telecommunication and radio stations, the military was able to capture the Palace of Miraflores. Castro León has publicly promised to eliminate subversive elements within Venezuela by establishing a temporary junta to enact his “5 National Points”, a proposed reorganization of the nation's constitution. While the military and the oligarchs firmly support Castro León, many Venezuelans are uncertain about the end goal of his “reorganization.”
strings.VEN_news.12.c: A dangerous individual of unknown quantity.
strings.VEN_news.10.desc:
A sigh of relief could be heard across Venezuela today, as the country has narrowly avoided another military coup. General Jesús María Castro León, a staunch critic of the country's left-leaning President, attempted to seize several of Venezuela's government institutions. However, due to a lack of communication between the barracks, the coup was halted by a combined police and military effort.

Following the attempt, General Castro León stood down and was taken into custody, justifying his actions as “in defence of the country he loves.” While the general surrendered, his co-conspirators have scattered. Several officers have been arrested in the aftermath, while others have fled abroad. Some suspect that the plot has simply moved underground, with this being only the first boulder in an avalanche that may yet come.
strings.VEN_news.10.b: Venezuelan democracy seems to be built to last.
strings.VEN_news.10.c: A failure in all things he attempted to do.
strings.VEN_news.13.desc:
The strained relationship between the Venezuelan government and Armed Forces came to a head today, as the country narrowly avoided a military coup. This attempt, led by General Castro León's protégé, Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal, has left hundreds around Caracas wounded, and the nation shaken.

After seizing the White Palace, the coup plotters entered a bitter skirmish with protesters and military police over the Palace of Miraflores, which gave the government time to mobilize loyal units. Though Moncada Vidal's forces were eventually pushed back, the use of artillery against Miraflores and other areas of Urdaneta Avenue has left the capital scarred. Once again Venezuela is haunted by her military past, which she seems to never be able to shake.
strings.VEN_news.13.a: Playing dictator in America's sandpit will always end up with sand in your eyes.
strings.VEN_news.13.b: A brutal last strike by the worst of the Armed Forces.
strings.VEN_news.13.c: Moncada Vidal's remaining dogs best scurry off to the jungle.
strings.VEN_news.14.desc:
The strained relationship between the Venezuelan government and Armed Forces came to a head today, as General Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal has seized power. President Rafael Caldera's negotiations over the Essequibo, which drew the ire of nationalistic military officers, seems to have been the last straw.

Moncada Vidal - protégé of the retired General Jesús María Castro León - is the leader of this nationalist clique. Seizing the Palace of Miraflores in what spectators are calling a violent and ferocious assault, Moncada Vidal and his radical followers, nicknamed “the Bolivarians,” have made several bold proclamations of changes to come. Though the future remains uncertain, it appears that Venezuela's young democracy has come to an end.
strings.VEN_news.14.a: Patriotism and pragmatism are not completely dead in Venezuela, then.
strings.VEN_news.14.c: The Organization of Free Nations does not take kindly to tyrants.
strings.VEN_news.47.t: {get_newspaper_header}The End of the National Governing Board
strings.VEN_news.47.desc:
The seeming last hope for Venezuela has spluttered out abruptly and without ceremony as the National Governing Board, the interim council constructed by Jesús María Castro León before his death, has been dissolved by force today following a violent revolt in the nation's capital.

Speculators have long expected tension between the board and the increasingly radicalised military. However, it seems the supplanting of the former dictator's protégé in favor of entrepeneur and philantropist Eugenio Mendoza struck too deep of a nerve in the Bolivarian clique of the military to be ignored.

The presidency has been reassumed by the military, now under the leadership of Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal. Moncada Vidal is a well-known nationalist ideologue, reputed for his fierce doctrinal rule over the military and authoritarian tendencies. Internationally, many worry what this will mean for Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.47.b: A brutal end for men only trying their best in trying times.
strings.VEN_news.47.c: Breaking treaties with us will cost dearly.
strings.VEN_news.28.desc:
Military rule continues in Venezuela as Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal, protégé and right hand man of the former dictator Jesús María Castro León, has been named his successor. Though the General long claimed an eventual return to democracy, it appears the failed implementation of his 5 Point Plan caused him to reconsider.

Moncada Vidal is well known within military circles for his fervent, radical and ultranationalist approach and belief in the need for national renewal across Venezuela's political scene. Though his dedicated followers have done much to burnish Moncada Vidal's image within the populace and barracks, many Venezuelans express concern about his aggressive stance at home and abroad. Nevertheless, a grand parade throughout Caracas celebrated the nation's new leader.
strings.VEN_news.28.a: A man driven by his commitment is always welcome.
strings.VEN_news.28.b: A man whose intentions remain unknowable.
strings.VEN_news.28.c: El Cabito has signed Venezuela's death warrant.
strings.VEN_news.29.desc:
In news coming shortly after the retirement of General Jesús María Castro León from Venezuela's government, a National Governing Council has been created to act as an interim authority to begin the transfer of power from the military to civilian hands. Led by Eugenio Mendoza, Castro León's designated successor, the Council seeks radical reforms to undo the excesses caused by the military's overwhelming presence Venezuelan institutions.

Specifically, a recent programme leaked to the media has highlighted the need for a sharp reduction of radical elements within the military and the removal Bolivarian influence. Supporters of Mendoza believe these are necessary steps to see Venezuela return to both stability and democracy, while critics have alternated between labelling him as a puppet of the oligarch, or as a crypto-communist seeking to poison Venezuela with “international capital.”
strings.VEN_news.29.a: Hopefully, a man with his head screwed on tighter than his predecessors.
strings.VEN_news.29.b: Venezuela has called upon its brightest and boldest.
strings.VEN_news.29.c: A skilled statesman and excellent politician.
strings.VEN_news.30.t: {get_newspaper_header}The End of the National Governing Board
strings.VEN_news.30.desc:
What once acted as the seeming last hope for Venezuela in its darkest decade has spluttered out abruptly and without ceremony as the National Governing Board, the interim council constructed by Jesús María Castro León before his death, has been dissolved by force today following another military coup.

President Eugenio Mendoza resigned following the military dissolution of the council today, citing his inability to restore order and stability to the nation and apologising to the Venezuelan people. In his place, a longterm peer of General Castro León, Oscar Tamayo Suárez, is expected to lead an interim military junta, focused on restoring stability to the nation.

Tamayo Suárez is a known quantity in Venezuela and political force within the former government. Many point, however, to this likely leading to months - or worse - years, of continued inaction on the suspended state of the nation.
strings.VEN_news.30.a: Dragged and forgotten, the Generals take back what's rightfully theirs.
strings.VEN_news.30.b: A thin ray of hope, dashed.
strings.VEN_news.30.c: The breaking of our treaty cannot stand.
strings.VEN_news.31.desc: modern venezuela bill reorganized, oligarchs led by pedro tinoco soft coup mendoza and make him an oligarch puppet, fake democracy. woe is me.
strings.VEN_news.31.a: A fabrication that serves the interests of fat oligarchs.
strings.VEN_news.31.b: Mendoza once again calls on his disciples.
strings.VEN_news.31.c: It is shameful to cast doubts...
strings.VEN_news.32.desc: whulsum mendoza overpowers his enemies and does oligarchic liberalism paradise
strings.VEN_news.32.a: Another democratic project? Only a fool trips over the same stone twice.
strings.VEN_news.32.b: Much is promised, delivering on those promises is the issue.
strings.VEN_news.32.c: A promising event, let's hope it's followed through.
strings.VEN_news.34.desc:
Eugenio Mendoza, leader and richest man of Venezuela announced his resignation on a short but firm national broadcast today, citing “health issues and personal matters”. The position of head of state is now filled by his Minister of Internal Affairs, Pedro Tinoco, a wealthy businessman known for his in-depth relationship with the current regime.

Many pundits and international observers saw this move coming following the reorganization of the Modern Venezuela Bill, which promised a return to free elections, threatening the powerbases of many of the oligarchs who supported Mendoza. It is suspected that these oligarchs and magnates forced Mendoza to “retire” by threatening to support a military coup against him. It is unclear what direction Venezuela will take now, but one thing is clear: the power of the oligarchy will not be challenged.
strings.VEN_news.34.a: Outpaced by the greed of his compatriots.
strings.VEN_news.34.b: A titan in Venezuelan history - fallen.
strings.VEN_news.34.c: A sad end for a titan of a man.
strings.VEN_news.35.desc:
Eugenio Mendoza, leader and richest man of Venezuela, has announced new elections scheduled for 1970 on a national broadcast. Immediately, celebrations have broken out across the country in most cities and metropolitan regions. Cheered by the move, liberal dissidents forced abroad by General Castro León's coup have also begun making their way home.

These changes come as a result of Mendoza's Modern Venezuela Bill, legislation opposed both by military conspirators and many business magnates of the National Governing Board. However, with the passing of the bill, the most radical elements of the military have either been removed or cowed, while the opposing oligarchs look to the next election as a chance to rebuild their power structures.
strings.VEN_news.35.a: Another democracy built on the black veins of Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.35.b: A reliable trade partner for the future to come.
strings.VEN_news.35.c: Working alongside such a figure was a pleasure.
strings.VEN_news.36.desc:
Pedro Tinoco, an elite lawyer and banker, was sworn in today following Venezuela's first elections since General Castro León's coup in 1964. His inaugural address promised stability and prosperity for Venezuelans, backed by sensible macroeconomic management and infrastructure spending.

Tinoco's Integración Republicana received support from Venezuela's businessmen and industrialists, and the noted developmentalist has named leading executives to his cabinet.

Most observers attribute IR's electoral dominance to advantages rendered by the 'Modern Venezuela Bill', which was heavily amended by Tinoco and his associates on the National Governing Board. Eugenio Mendoza, a prominent former member of the Board who had called for free elections, could not be reached for comment.
strings.VEN_news.36.a: Finally - a man who understands the value of what his nation sits on.
strings.VEN_news.36.b: A man surely apt of business, though lacking in morals.
strings.VEN_news.36.c: Making Venezuela a whore to the highest bidder...?
strings.VEN_news.37.t: {get_newspaper_header}Arturo Uslar Pietri Inaugurated as Venezuelan President
strings.VEN_news.37.desc:
With the results of Venezuela's first free election since its military coup and return to democracy finally counted, it seems that Arturo Uslar Pietri has won a firm majority, allowing him to become President and putting his National Democratic Front into power. A noted artist and intellectual, as well as a political moderate, Uslar Pietri is widely expected by observers to use his first term to expand on civil liberties in tandem with economic liberalisation.

However, sceptics are concerned regarding whether or not these ambitions will actually bear fruit, citing the outsized impact that Venezuela's oligarchs had on his campaign, and how their aid was vital to his success. The question of oligarchical influence seeping into the actual running of government remains in the air, flaunted loudly by the opposition, despite a quiet gratitude for the return of democracy.
strings.VEN_news.37.a: A new Republic as fragile as the old one.
strings.VEN_news.37.b: A pawn, too simple — too naive — to realize.
strings.VEN_news.37.c: A man we can work with.
strings.VEN_news.38.desc:
Venezuelan political heavyweight Jóvito Villalba has won a stunning victory today, finally taking the presidency after previous failed attempts. With the end of Mendoza's government and a restoration of democracy, Villalba's success has been credited to the growing backlash against oligarchic control in the country. His victory comes as a surprise given the colossal electoral advantages that the rival party, Frente Nacional Democrático, possessed.

Though Villalba briefly fled the country after the Easter Coup, he remained leader of the URD party in exile. After returning to Venezuela he created a big-tent coalition, riding a wave of popular discontent against the governing elites. Villalba is expected to re-establish ties with Venezuela's old allies in the Veracruz Pact.
strings.VEN_news.38.a: An old titan, well past his prime.
strings.VEN_news.38.c: A most warm friendship, even in such troubling times.
strings.VEN_news.17.desc:
In the wake of military ideologue Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal's seizure of power in Venezuela, a so-called “Bolivarian Republic” has been declared, formally ending the Fourth Republic.

The new government, under the leadership of the highly nationalistic Bolivarian Military Civic Union, has denounced the imperialism they claim has plagued Venezuela for decades, stating that the formation of this Republic signifies an end to the nation's humiliation.

Many within the Organization of Free Nations and Veracruz Pact have urged strong condemnations for what is becoming an increasingly insular, totalitarian and xenophobic regime. Within Venezuela, the declaration has been marked by vibrant military parades and a day of national celebration.
strings.VEN_news.17.a: A promising return from the decay of the last few years.
strings.VEN_news.17.b: A dangerous, unstable and radical idea.
strings.VEN_news.17.c: Bolívar was felled once, and died a long death, and will do so again.
strings.VEN_news.40.t: {get_newspaper_header}Venezuelan Government Prevails in Dance of the Dogs
strings.VEN_news.40.desc:
After massive, months-long riots and demonstrations, the Bolivarian government of Venezuela has prevailed and strengthened their grip on the nation. The socialist movement has nearly been exterminated, with the small remnants forced to go into hiding in urban centers or the Andes. Exiled democratic politicians have condemned the “wanton bloodshed” to no visible effect.

While the intensification of the riots led to a coup attempt by a radical dissident Bolivarian faction led by Nicolás Hurtado Barrios, the coup failed completely, leading to the execution of its leaders and several other opposition figures. Appearances by the regime's leader, Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal have grown less frequent, with younger, more zealous officers taking on larger roles. Regardless of who is truly in charge of the South American pariah state, the Bolivarian Revolution has been cemented.
strings.VEN_news.40.b: A tiny sailboat amongst a river of blood.
strings.VEN_news.40.c: The chaos of that cursed regime lingers on.
strings.VEN_news.41.t: {get_newspaper_header}July Coup in The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela
strings.VEN_news.41.desc:
Following domestic turmoil after the violent nationalization of foreign-owned oil assets, indiscriminate massacres conducted by Bolivarian paramilitaries and the complete severance of ties with the United States, dissident Bolivarian forces within the regime have appeared to take advantage of its woes, sieging the Miraflores Palace and executing President Moncada Vidal on live television to calm widespread rioting.

The leader of the coup, Nicolás Hurtado Barrios, later appeared in an address where he announced a programme of land reform and economic redistribution. While still a committed Bolivarian and participant in the White Palace Revolution, Hurtado Barrios is considered the leader of the relative “left” faction of the junta, associated with a peasantist and populist power base, both of whom have helped calm rioting since his takeover and redirected the anger towards America.
strings.VEN_news.41.a: A full circle of nationalism, decline and decay.
strings.VEN_news.41.b: From ideology to ideology she has been tossed.
strings.VEN_news.41.c: The Bolivarian engine turns a wheel.
strings.VEN_news.69.desc:
In shocking news today, the Presidents of Venezuela and Colombia announced in a joint speech the unification of their respective nations to reform the Bolivarian Republic of Gran Colombia. They stated the creation of the new state was to ward off foreign imperialism, particularly from the United States.

Already, the drafting of a new constitution is underway, as both militaries launch joint parades to commemorate the occasion. More pressingly, the new Republic has sent communiques to neighbors inviting them to become part of the new state. International observers are fearful that the new regional power may choose to forcefully annex them into the Republic. Superpowers wait and watch for what will happen to South America, as the duopoly of Argentina and Brazil is challenged like never before.
strings.VEN_news.69.a: A rottweiler let loose in America's backyard.
strings.VEN_news.69.c: A threat to freedom across the continent.
strings.VEN_news.62.desc:
War erupted today as the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela launched an invasion to seize the disputed Essequibo region from neighboring Guyana. Its soldiers aim to march to the Essequibo river, covering roughly two-thirds of Guyana's territory to conquer a Spanish imperial claim.

The dispute persisted for decades due to nationalism and a longstanding disagreement between the British and Gran Colombia. The emergence of the militaristic, ultranationalist and fascist Bolivarian Republic in Venezuela only heightened tensions.

Already, Guyana, a long-standing member of the Organization of Free Nations, has called its allies to arms. Though the response of OFN forces to mobilize has been slow, being caught by surprise, many expect the campaign to end poorly for the Bolivarian Republic.
strings.VEN_news.62.b: A feud that far outdates both nations.
strings.VEN_news.62.c: And so, the hammer will come down on the Bolivarians.
strings.VEN_news.63.desc:
Venezuelan forces have succeeded in seizing the disputed Essequibo region from Guyana in a full-scale invasion. With a disorganized and unprepared Guyanese army and Canadian garrison, the OFN failed to mobilize rapidly enough to defend the small nation.

Mounting casualties and a failed counteroffensives have forced Canada and the United States to the negotiating table, allowing Venezuela to annex the Essequibo in exchange for the establishment of a Eastern Guyana rump state. Surinamese forces, vital in defending their neighbor, have helped instate a temporary junta while the Canadian authorities organize what remains of Guyana. The move has largely reinforced Venezuela's status as an international pariah in the Americas, but has been met with rapturous nationalist reception at home.
strings.VEN_news.63.a: The Organization of Free Nations licks its wounds.
strings.VEN_news.63.b: What ever happened to the Monroe Doctrine?
strings.VEN_news.63.c: A show of incredible, shocking and, worst of all, humiliating might.
strings.VEN_news.64.desc:
Recent domestic conflict in Venezuela has evolved into civil war, following the failure of the Bolivarian regime's invasion of Guyana and the subsequent assasination of President Moncada Vidal. Escalating communist insurgencies against the incumbent Bolivarians have led the OAS to intervene against both parties to restore stability.

With a three-way conflict between the Bolivarianist Republic, the communist insurgents, and the OAS interventionary force extending across rough terrain, peace is not anticipated to return soon. The open use of the American military in this conflict has drawn criticism from some Latin American intellectuals, who argue that the show of force is to cow other potential “troublemakers” into submission.
strings.VEN_news.64.a: A more... direct approach than usual.
strings.VEN_news.67.desc:
To the surprise of many, the government of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela led by Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal's successor, Manuel Azuaje Ortega, has managed to become the sole authority over Venezuela once again. Having conducted a vicious and extensive extermination campaign against the communist revolutionaries of the FALN, they also decisively pushed the OAS-OFN joint invasion back into the sea and over the border with Guyana, securing full control over national territory.

In his first speech since the victory, Azuaje Ortega proclaimed a full mobilization against remaining enemies of the state within Venezuela. The OAS has furiously condemned him as a tyrant, but its failed intervention is already being seen as a serious blow to the organization's prestige and capabilities.
strings.VEN_news.67.b: The pariah state that refuses to be a pariah.
strings.VEN_news.67.c: The engine of Bolivarianism continues to be fueled with the blood of its kinsmen.
strings.VEN_news.66.desc:
Against all odds, the communist movement of FALN - Bandera Roja has managed to overthrow the Bolivarian Republic and drive out the invading OAS-OFN task force. International observers attribute their victory to ample popular support and the ability to mobilize overwhelming numbers. Nationalist backlash against the OAS intervention drove revolts across Venezuela's urban centers, which lead to government buildings being ransacked and the lynching of officials accused of 'collaboration'.

Américo Silva, leader of the group, has proclaimed the establishment of the People's Republic of Venezuela and a people's mobilization against counterrevolutionary enemies inside the government's territory. His success may inspire similar movements within Venezuela's neighbors and across the Americas.
strings.VEN_news.66.c: How could we have let this happen?
strings.VEN_news.65.desc:
After an arduous campaign, the OFN-OAS joint forces have successfully ended their pacification of Venezuela. Soldiers across the Americas and the OFN celebrate as they are shipped back to their home countries, though the reaction of Venezuelan civilians has been apathetic at best. As the pariah state was liberated, footage and evidence showed all manner of atrocities from torture centers and concentration camps to mass graves and ghost towns.

The work of the task force now shifts to preparing the country for a return to self-government and democracy, as the Latin American nation works to rebuild its institutions, trial remaining regime figures, and remove extant fascist influence in favor of OFN-aligned values. While both communist and Bolivarian resistance remains in the countryside, peace has returned to Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.65.a: The winner writes history it seems.
strings.VEN_news.65.b: At the very least, it's over.
strings.VEN_news.48.t: {get_newspaper_header}Enrique Tejera París Assumes Control of Venezuela
strings.VEN_news.48.desc:
With the beginning of the Oil Crisis and the worldwide financial shock, the OAS administration of Venezuela has, after pressure from the United States, officially ended. Power is currently being transferred to Dr. Enrique Tejera París, a leader of the democratic movement-in-exile in the U.S. with limited popularity in Venezuela. Pacification campaigns in the countryside continue against Bolivarian and communist insurgents, as the nation slowly rebuilds itself.

Though OAS rule has ended, significant American presence remains, with Venezuela confirmed as an official OFN member. Sporadic protests have occurred in the U.S. against the continued occupation, though the response in Caracas and Maracaibo has been muted.
strings.VEN_news.48.a: Another lapdog to add to America's collection.
strings.VEN_news.49.desc:
Venezuela has descended into civil war after a massive communist uprising by the Armed Forces of National Liberation, or FALN, failed to oust the government. Despite the FALN's overwhelming numbers, the national army managed to regroup and oust organized FALN forces from coastal regions and plains.

Internal pressures and communism's spread in Latin America have radicalized much of Venezuela's population, allowing the FALN to recoup its losses. Already, fresh troops are gathering at its makeshift capital of Ciudad Bolívar, as bloodied survivors of its initial assault gather in the Andes. Compounding the government's difficulties are sabotage campaigns by radical students and insurgent bands in reclaimed rural areas.
strings.VEN_news.49.b: The llanos stained with reds' blood.
strings.VEN_news.49.c: Venezuela has more communists than it has oil!
strings.VEN_news.50.desc:
Military parades were held simultaneously in Caracas, Maracaibo, and Ciudad Bolívar to celebrate the defeat of the communists in Venezuela's grueling civil war. During the Caracas event, Marcos Pérez Jiménez proceeded down the 'System of Nationality' promenade to lay a wreath at the monument to Venezuela's deceased heroes, before launching into a passionate speech promising rapid development to repair the damages of the failed revolution and enrich those who fought for their nation.

Pérez Jiménez is anticipated to reach out to his foreign backers, key in the war effort, to capitalize these ventures. To reassure investors, the robust state security apparatus built by Pérez Jiménez acolyte Pedro Estrada is hunting down the few members of the FALN politbureau that remain at large.
strings.VEN_news.50.a: Dead communists and oil. All one can hope for from Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.50.b: The New National Ideal triumphs over international revolution.
strings.VEN_news.50.c: Coups, revolutions, nothing can keep Pérez Jiménez down.
strings.VEN_news.51.desc:
Members of Venezuela's National Governing Board were present in Caracas and Maracaraibo today to pay respects to troops returning home from the long campaigns to defeat the FALN. The Board's chair announced an increase in pensions for war widows and the wounded, a symbolic measure aimed at those who accuse its elite members of failing to stem the inequality that led to widespread FALN support.

A more detailed policy program is expected in the coming days. A leaked draft suggests that the Board will double down on the developmentalist strategy it pursued prior to the failed revolution, but pursue closer ties with its foreign backers to secure the financing needed to repair oil and transportation infrastructure damaged in the conflict. The leak from the highest echelons of the Board suggests internal disunity following the chaos of the war.
strings.VEN_news.51.a: They can fling their coin around all they like. But keep a firm grip on the gun.
strings.VEN_news.51.b: Venezuela is the country of conceited nonentities and enshrined reputations.
strings.VEN_news.51.c: Invest across the Caribbean? We'd be buying low...
strings.VEN_news.52.desc:
Sober military parades were held throughout Venezuela's major cities today before troops filed back to their barracks. The muted celebrations commemorated the final defeat of the FALN, which at points nearly won the nation's devastating civil war. General Pablo Antonio Flores assumed control over Venezuela after the nation's civilian administration became discredited by its inability to prosecute the war.

Flores, in attendance at the Caracas event, proceeded down the Paseo Los Próceres promenade to lay a wreath in honor of those who died in the conflict. A short speech followed in which the general reiterated his promise that a swift and effective national reconstruction would allow a return to democracy in 1973. The general pledged to then retire from public life.
strings.VEN_news.52.a: The communists will return as soon as they lighten the yoke.
strings.VEN_news.53.desc:
Popular celebrations broke out across Venezuela today, from the dormitories of Central University to isolated plains hamlets, as Gustavo Machado of the Communist Party announced the total victory of the Armed Forces of National Liberation. The last extant forces of the Venezuelan military, hamstrung by sabotage, guerilla attacks on their rear, and defections in the wake of the Caracas government's crisis of legitimacy, surrendered in the face of overwhelming numbers.

Amidst energetic joropo music, communist agitators announce to crowds the coming nationalization of the oil industry and ambitious land reform. Despite the movement's apparent popularity, many Venezuelans have taken refuge in their homes or churches, fearful of coming turmoil. Latin American states and oil firms have reacted with similar trepidation, condemning revolutionary seizures and violence.
strings.VEN_news.53.a: A hateful outcome. But at least the Americans will be kept busy fighting the disease.
strings.VEN_news.53.b: What's going to happen to all that oil?
strings.VEN_news.53.c: An ignorant people is a blind instrument of their own destruction.
strings.VEN_news.54.desc:
Venezuelan troops escorted captured members of the FALN politbureau to Caracas today, where they are expected to stand trial for treason. The communist revolutionaries nearly overthrew Venezuela's democratically elected government at the start of the nation's civil war, but firm action by the nation's military and support from the United States and Veracruz Pact allies steadily drove the rebels back.

In a televised address from Miraflores Palace, President {ven_getleader} mourned the immense loss of life and vowed to rebuild a more just Venezuela, one free of the specter of communism. Noting that towns, families, and friends had been divided by the conflict, he called for a spirit of reinvigorated brotherhood, referencing Bolívar's adage “Unity makes everything possible; we must preserve that precious principle.”
strings.VEN_news.54.c: A veritable Lincoln of the tropics.
strings.VEN_news.55.desc:
The Condor Legion, the armed Latin American fascist youth organization, has claimed responsibility for the assasination of Venezuelan Communist Party leader Gustavo Machado and for a bomb attack on his state funeral. While the bomb itself killed few, FALN paramilitaries, unsure of the nature of the threat, opened fire on the panicking crowd.

The elderly Machado had been a unifying figure for revolutionary Venezuela, and was respected in far-left circles across Latin America for his role in founding the communist parties of Cuba and France. With his absence and the subsequent disaster at the funeral, analysts predict a worsening of factionalism within the Politbureau and on the streets. Already, various leaders of guerilla groups during the Revolution have expressed outrage over the egregious security failures, with some seeking to rearm their men against domestic and international rightists.
strings.VEN_news.55.a: Soak the Condor's beak in blood.
strings.VEN_news.55.b: Killing the man, and his idea?
strings.VEN_news.55.c: And not a word about the FBI. Well-done, team.
strings.VEN_news.59.t: {get_newspaper_header}Pedro Ortega Díaz Assumes Control in Venezuela
strings.VEN_news.57.t: {get_newspaper_header}Eduardo Gallegos Mancera Inaugurated as Venezuelan President
strings.VEN_news.57.desc: machado resigns, gallegos becomes president representing old guard
strings.VEN_news.68.desc: machado resigns, petkoff becomes president representing new guard
strings.VEN_news.70.desc:
Today in the city of Cúcuta, the Presidents of Venezuela and Colombia proclaimed the creation of the People's Republic of Gran Colombia, a nod to the once-thought-lost Bolivarian dream. This united Republic was enabled by the success of the Venezuelan communist revolution and the victory of the Colombian Revolutionary Union against its enemies in the Colombian Civil War, and the subsequent consolidation of their leftist regimes.

Party members and the revolutionary armed forces have launched parades across the newly reunified nation as the states begin the lengthy process of integrating.

International reception to this development ranges from cold to actively hostile, with many governments condemning the new Republic's alleged 'invitation' to neighboring countries to join the pact.
strings.VEN_news.70.a: An unkempt backyard full of weeds.
strings.VEN_news.70.c: A matter to be dealt with in the future.
strings.VEN_news.33.desc:
Following an extended period of military rule in Venezuela, the incumbent Junta has announced its own dissolution in favor of an interim civilian government. However, opposition figures have already made sceptical remarks regarding the credibility of the incoming government, citing the overbearing presence of Luis Felipe Llovera Páez, a figure of some notoriety due to his involvement in the 1948 coup against President Rómulo Gallegos.

Others have questioned Llovera Páez's connections to the deposed dictator, Marcos Pérez Jiménez, and have publicly questioned whether or not the ex-Caudillo will be allowed to return to Venezuela. Llovera Páez's silence on the matter in the face of intense scrutiny has led to many assuming his return is imminent once a sufficient level of stability is restored to the fractured nation.
strings.VEN_news.33.a: A caretaker to take care of the rabble.
strings.VEN_news.33.b: Another temporary suspension of freedom to add to the pile.
strings.VEN_news.39.desc:
The unending turmoil of Venezuela seems to have only further evolved today as yet another faction has clawed its way into power within the governing Military Junta. Following the sudden assasination of General Oscar Tamayo Suárez by supposed communist agitators, Roberto Casanova, Minister of Defense, has stepped in to lead the Junta.

Some claim supposed government interference that was truly responsible for General Tamayo's death. Casanova has, however, reportedly used the opportunity to react with a brutal crackdown on the recognized opposition cliques as an act of retaliation. Owing to Casanova's long service in the cabinet of former dictator Marcos Pérez Jiménez, many speculators suggest that his rise to office will only act as interim for the former dictator's inevitable return. However, such a move requires far more unity that Casanova seems to currently hold over his own government.
strings.VEN_news.39.a: They couldn't live with their own failure, it led them back to him.
strings.VEN_news.39.b: Old tricks from the same man.
strings.VEN_news.42.desc:
To the surprise of few, Marcos Pérez Jiménez has been given a state welcome on his return to Venezuela today, greeted off the plane from Iberia by noted ally General Luis Felipe Llovera Páez. Llovera Páez is expected to announce his resignation as President to pave the way for Pérez Jiménez to be inaugurated, with the general to be named Minister of Internal Affairs.

International observers predict Pérez Jiménez will employ the developmentalist and repressive measures that characterized his previous authoritarian government. Already, embassies in Caracas have received requests for asylum from notable dissident figures.
strings.VEN_news.42.a: A scarce few years before they went running back to their master.
strings.VEN_news.42.b: And yet, she chose him again? Perhaps, he truly is destined.
strings.VEN_news.42.c: Democracy was suffocated in her cradle.
strings.VEN_news.46.desc:
An unknown communist assailant fired shots against Marcos Pérez Jiménez during a military parade today in Caracas, before being quickly apprehended. However, Pérez Jiménez has fallen into a deep coma. Rushed to get medical help, his prognosis indicates that he is likely to be incapacitated for some time.

Pérez Jiménez's comatose state is likely to facilitate a growing factionalism within the government. Though information is scarce, it seems there is a plot to depose the ailing dictator.

Luis Felipe Llovera Páez, the Minister of Internal Affairs and a confidante to Pérez Jiménez, has already been sworn in as Interim President. Only time will tell if Llovera Páez and his fellow loyalists will be able to preserve Pérez Jiménez in power while he is indisposed.
strings.VEN_news.46.a: Just desserts for the Iron Tyrant.
strings.VEN_news.46.b: Whatever you think of the dictator, think more of Venezuela's future.
strings.VEN_news.46.c: The guns of the jungle finally found their target.
strings.VEN_news.43.desc:
Following a failed plot by the Seguridad Nacional's chief Pedro Estrada and the Minister of Finance Laureano Vallenilla Planchart to depose the comatose Pérez Jiménez and his second-in-command, Luis Felipe Llovera Páez, the 'Iron Tyrant' has returned and regained control of the country.

Venezuela's security services and other areas of the state have been purged, with the returned President citing their treason and incompetence as rationale. In parallel, a major crackdown on the underground opposition movement both inside and outside Venezuela has begun, with key figures being targeted for assassination. Leaked documents indicate cooperation with the fascist Condor Legion to accomplish this. According to international observers, Pérez Jiménez's hold has only solidified after this crisis.
strings.VEN_news.43.a: They tried, failed, and he still remains.
strings.VEN_news.43.b: A foundation stabilized with thousands of bodies.
strings.VEN_news.44.desc:
After tense weeks with little news from Venezuela, Margot Pérez Jiménez-Chalbaud, daughter of the former Venezuelan dictator, has announced the death of her father after an assassination attempt left him in a coma. A reorganization of the Venezuelan government is already underway and has noticeably purged many loyalists to the late tyrant, among them Luis Felipe Llovera Páez, formerly the Interim President.

Pedro Estrada, the Seguridad Nacional's chief, in cooperation with Minister of Finance Laureano Vallenilla Planchart, swiftly rallied the Civic National Crusade and Senate to install Margot in her father's place. The intelligence chief is expected to dominate the inexperienced Pérez Jiménez-Chalbaud's government. Estrada's dark reputation has some diplomats whispering that Pérez Jiménez's assasination may have been at his hands.
strings.VEN_news.44.a: Weak fools hiding behind a skirt.
strings.VEN_news.44.b: Caesar is gone, yet his assassins remain clueless.
strings.VEN_news.44.c: One firm kick, and the rotten structure will fall.
strings.VEN_news.19.desc:
A small miracle has occurred for the Democratic Republican Union it seems, as following the disastrous Presidency of Fabricio Ojeda, they have found themselves reelected with a narrow margin. Many have speculated the divisive campaigns of Democratic Action and COPEI contributed to this bizarre development.

Francisco Arreaza Arreaza, the political protégé of the party's chairman Jóvito Villalba enters Miraflores today on a promise of stability and prosperity, promising a calm maintenance of the status quo. This seems to have struck some type of accord with the national conscience, though detractors of the regime accuse Arreaza of being little more than a figurehead for Villalba's continued political vision.

Regardless, Venezuela is one to watch.
strings.VEN_news.19.a: Another of Villalba's golden boys, tied by his puppet strings.
strings.VEN_news.19.b: The party of good governance, it seems.
strings.VEN_news.19.c: Respect and discipline will always make party politics better than populism.
strings.VEN_news.20.t: {get_newspaper_header}Alirio Ugarte Pelayo Inaugurated as Venezuelan President
strings.VEN_news.20.desc:
Crowds gather in Caracas today as Alirio Ugarte Pelayo is inaugurated as President of Venezuela. A smoking Ugarte assured his supporters that a political transformation would soon begin. Promises he made during the campaign such as healthcare, education, and welfare reform, appear forthcoming.

Born the bastard son of the caudillo José Gabaldón, Alirio's rise from the lowest of Venezuelan society has been nothing short of inspirational. Building a reputation as an intellectual and orator over the last decade, his ideas have helped transform the Unión Republicana Democrática.

For today, at least, the people of Venezuela celebrate, and let out a small sigh of relief.
strings.VEN_news.20.a: Bastards will do as bastards do.
strings.VEN_news.20.b: An amicable, sensible man in a turbulent time.
strings.VEN_news.20.c: Let's hope he is more collected than his predecessor.
strings.VEN_news.21.desc:
Venezuela has chosen its next leader, as Miguel Ángel Burelli Rivas ascends to the Presidency of the Republic. A renowned statesman, businessman and linguist, Burelli carries the torch of Jóvito Villalba and the Unión Republicana Democrática party's liberal traditions.

Having previously served as Foreign Minister, Burelli has earned a reputation as an internationalist and a deal maker. In his victory speech, the new President promised that pragmatic diplomacy and continued economic prosperity would be his core policy objectives.

As the Republic of Venezuela enters a new chapter, its people remain optimistic about their government and their future.
strings.VEN_news.21.a: Hands greased thickly with oil win out above real politics again.
strings.VEN_news.21.b: A careerist will always find a home in Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.21.c: A known quantity, and good news.
strings.VEN_news.22.t: {get_newspaper_header}Reinaldo Leandro Mora Inaugurated as Venezuelan President
strings.VEN_news.22.desc:
Elections have come to an end in Venezuela, and the candidate of the Acción Democrática party, Reinaldo Leandro Mora, has emerged victorious in the race for the presidency.

Having served for nearly two decades in the civil service, the foreign office, and as a congressman, few men can claim to be more experienced than the new President. During his campaign, Leandro Mora outlined plans to not only reinvigorate Venezuela's oil industry, but promote growth across the nation.

Few are certain what this next decade brings, but many Venezuelans believe their country is in safe hands.
strings.VEN_news.22.a: Yet another feckless careerist, no surprise.
strings.VEN_news.22.b: The man's reputation precedes him, we hope for great things.
strings.VEN_news.22.c: Seems to be a measured man of great repute.
strings.VEN_news.23.desc:
Tragedies strike thrice in Venezuela as, for the third time in two decades, a national leader is assassinated for the whole nation to see. Earlier today, Alirio Ugarte Pelayo, the helmsman of the ruling Democratic Republican Union party, was assassinated.

Though Alirio may have proved a controversial figure within his own party, nationally he enjoyed widespread public support. It was during a visit to the Ministry of Defense, meant to secure support for his ministry, that a young army lieutenant would shoot him, delivering wounds that would place the President in a critical condition, with him passing in the early hours of the next morning.

Venezuela's institutions lie in disarray, and much like the death of Rómulo Betancourt years before, few can predict what comes next.
strings.VEN_news.23.a: Socialists will always tear themselves to shreds.
strings.VEN_news.23.b: A man who served his country well, to the bitter end.
strings.VEN_news.24.t: {get_newspaper_header}Carlos Andrés Pérez Inaugurated as Venezuelan President
strings.VEN_news.24.desc:
Carlos Andrés Pérez was inaugurated as President of Venezuela today, representing a remarkable shift in the fortunes of Acción Democrática. After the party suffered a humiliating defeat in the 1963 election, Carlos Andrés Pérez, or CAP for short, brought it back to its popular, youthful roots.

Having joined the party in its early days as a student organizer, Carlos Andrés would make a name for himself through his charisma and fiery speeches. Now he has led the party to a historic victory.

The new President has positioned himself as a 20th century statesman, looking to grow the Venezuelan economy as well as battle the gripping inequality rife within it. AD supporters across the country now wait eagerly for the President's next moves as Venezuela steps into a new decade.
strings.VEN_news.24.a: A populist like him is not always what they seem.
strings.VEN_news.24.b: A towering figure against the meritocratic traditions of Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.24.c: A charming, reinvigorated figure - high hopes indeed.
strings.VEN_news.25.t: {get_newspaper_header}Luis Beltrán Prieto Figueroa Inaugurated as Venezuelan President
strings.VEN_news.25.desc:
A new chapter is made in the history of Venezuela's ruling party, Democratic Action, today as she turns a new page, one flooded with new dreams and new ideas.

Luis Beltrán Prieto Figueroa, a patriarch of Democratic Action since its inception, comes from a more left-leaning, egalitarian wing of the party, one that has long struggled for its place against the ruling Betancourtists. Riding a huge wave of public support for his policies and character, Prieto was able to win not only his party's nomination, but also the latest presidential election by a large margin.

This result will surely send ripples throughout Venezuela. For the first time since the death of her founder, AD has been reinvigorated, and holds the revolutionary flame aloft once again.
strings.VEN_news.25.a: Bowing to the pressure of the masses.
strings.VEN_news.25.b: A life spent fighting for the desperate and unprivileged.
strings.VEN_news.25.c: Acción Democrática opens a new chapter in its history.
strings.VEN_news.26.desc:
A vibrant campaign and a message of peace and unity, it seems, have prevailed against all challengers in Venezuela, as Rafael Caldera, veteran political operator and stalwart of Christian democratic values, has swept into the Presidency. A career spent in the political wilderness developed Caldera's reputation as a man of integrity and pragmatism, which has allowed him to lead his COPEI party to a historic victory.

Caldera has promised a renewed focus on agriculture and the rural sector while continuing to grow the economy. He also plans to resolve longstanding schisms between Venezuela and its neighbors, going so far as to propose negotiations with Guyana to resolve the Essequibo territorial dispute.
strings.VEN_news.26.a: Preferable to all their other poor options.
strings.VEN_news.26.c: A real powerhouse in Venezuela's politics.
strings.VEN_news.27.desc:
For the second time in a decade, the COPEI party has swept into power in Venezuela alongside its charismatic rising star, Lorenzo Fernández. A longtime ally and friend of former President Rafael Caldera, observers have said his victory represents a vote of approval for the programs and policies of the Social Christian party as a whole.

Certainly no veteran to party politics, Fernández's unique personal charm and reputation made him the logical choice to succeed Caldera. In addition to continuing the policies of his predecessor, Fernández has promised to expand free trade and enterprise across the nation, ushering in a new age of economic prosperity.
strings.VEN_news.27.a: And so, the rot has set in for Venezuela.
strings.VEN_news.27.b: A capable successor, and a skilled orator to boot.
strings.VEN_news.27.c: Fernández will help safeguard our shared interests.
strings.VEN_news.15.desc:
In one of the more shocking situations to come from Venezuela, the sitting President, Fabricio Ojeda, known for his leftist revolutionary views, has been ousted in what is being considered an internal government coup.

Ojeda's socialist revolutionary rhetoric was always controversial nationally as well as within his own party, the Democratic Republican Union, being forced to appease the party's liberal majority.

It would, however, be this same faction, led by chairman Jóvito Villalba, that would spell the downfall of the President. As the Senate and the Palace of Miraflores are engulfed in a sea of arguments regarding the path forward, Luis Augusto Dubuc, President of the Venezuelan Congress, has been appointed as interim President until the next Presidential elections.
strings.VEN_news.15.a: Poking at the eagle's talons will never result in less.
strings.VEN_news.15.b: Ambitions are one thing, delivery is another.
strings.VEN_news.15.c: Ojeda was spirited, though went too far in his aims...
strings.VEN_news.16.desc:
Alarming news from Venezuela today, as once again the Armed Forces have seized power. The coup plotters, led by General Félix Román Moreno, stormed the Presidential Palace and arrested sitting President Fabricio Ojeda, whose socialist platform was an anathema to the Perezjimenista-era officers of the Venezuelan military.

After months of rising tensions and increasing encroachment by the President on the military's hierarchy, General Román Moreno finally made his move, denouncing President Ojeda as a “national disgrace.” Though the fate of Ojeda is yet to be determined, few expect a fair trial. Already, the General has announced his desire for changes to be made to the Venezuelan constitution, to ensure the nation is never again entrusted to socialists.
strings.VEN_news.16.a: The ever-unquenchable fury of the Armed Forces.
strings.VEN_news.16.b: Venezuelan democracy never stood a chance.
strings.VEN_news.16.c: Pérez Jiménez's meddling will come back to bite him, sooner than he may think.
strings.VEN_news.60.desc:
Chaos and celebration in Caracas today as thousands of citizens thwart the second coup attempt against Venezuelan President Fabricio Ojeda by blocking the military's route to the National Assembly. Loyalist police, National Guard and military units used the delay to surround and arrest the conspirators, including President of the Congress Luis Augosto Dubuc and several legislators.

After fending off a military putsch in 1964, Ojeda's controversial push to nationalize Venezuela's oil industry united a broader coalition against him, including military nationalists, members of the opposition Acción Democrática, and the right-wing of his own Unión Republicana Democrática. Nevertheless, popular support and intelligence efforts by his Veracruz Pact allies overcame the threat. With key opponents now jailed and U.S. oil companies implicated, Ojeda's nationalization plans appear unstoppable.
strings.VEN_news.60.b: He can't keep getting away with it!
strings.VEN_news.60.c: Their own Cárdenas - a hero of the Veracruz Pact!
strings.VEN_news.60.d: At least there won't be blood.
strings.VEN_forpol.100.d:
The folder of embossed leather with a gold crest landed on the mahogany table with a dull, solid sound. It was not just a report - it was, in essence, a bill of sale for an entire country. The consolidated memorandum from the Foreign Ministry, the Ministry of Economy, and Iberian intelligence services read like the best poetry of the Golden Age: Venezuela, the prodigal daughter, had returned to the bosom of the family, and this time the leash in Iberian hands was shorter than ever.

At the center of the report towered the figure of the victor - Jesús María Castro León. A man of the old school who preferred the bitterness of voluntary exile to the humiliation of serving populists who had seized power. His swift dash from the misty hills of San Cristóbal to the gates of Caracas proved: steel is still stronger than demagoguery. Now, occupying the chair in Miraflores, the General wastes no time on empty speeches.

He has begun implementing his “Five National Points” - a grandiose surgical project to reshape the state. The new Constitution he is writing will not be a collection of liberal dreams, but a charter where the army becomes the backbone of the nation, and discipline - the law.

For Madrid and Lisbon, this means the dawn of an era of abundance. Venezuelan oil will flow into Spanish tankers, markets will open for Portuguese goods, and the strategic foothold in the Americas is now cemented tight. While the rest of the world looks with anxiety at the coming economic storms, Iberia has secured for itself the safest and richest haven.
strings.VEN_forpol.100.a: The investment paid off a hundredfold.
strings.VEN_forpol.102.desc:
Sunrise dawned in Caracas to the tune of a meticulously devised orchestra.

Carrying the chords were countless columns of APCs and military trucks riding along the main street toward the national assembly.

Curious onlookers found their approach barred through carefully placed roadblocks, and by the time confused loyalist units understood the meaning of this peculiar spectacle, it was already far too late to prevent its occurrence.

Like clockwork, opposition delegates pouring from a cortège of black Cadillacs descended upon a mostly empty Capitolio far earlier than its usual opening hours, and promptly declared an emergency session. Then, the choir began.

Just as he'd practiced, the URD spokesman proclaimed Fabricio Ojeda's presidency invalid on constitutional grounds, followed by a whole flow of accusations ranging from gross economic mismanagement to dangerous, undemocratic conduct.

One by one, all the dominoes fell right into place. The martial curfew. The reversal of the recent nationalization policies. The swift dismissal of any officer who could present a threat to the ongoing coup. And at last, the grand finale.

But only from the confines of the Cuban embassy, where he and his cabinet had hastily found shelter within, would the Venezuelan President learn of the unanimous results of the impeachment vote that had just been carried against him.

And his powerlessness to do anything about it.
strings.VEN_forpol.102.a: A magnificent ensemble, with Washington as its maestro.
strings.VEN_forpol.103.desc:
If one could embody the streets of Caracas on this particular day, they'd bear witness to not just one, but several spectacular displays.

They would first behold the morning break to military convoys waltzing along the main road toward the National Assembly.

By noon, they'd watch the same conspirators who had just poured from these trucks find their exit from the Capitolio swarmed by a tide of Ojedistas supporters. Then, faced with the realization that one of their missing pieces might have harbored slightly different aims.

Not long afterward, their arteries would ring with the sounds of an address from the nearby military headquarters, denouncing the illegitimacy of the self-proclaimed provisional government and condemning its illegal attempt at usurping power.

The following hours would see them painted with pictures of ferocious clashes, as both the coup's orchestrators and those objecting against it found their way into the clutch of rogue army units sent to restore order across the capital.

One by one, they'd attest to the cries of protestors being smothered by the blare of loudspeakers and, eventually, gunshots.

And when evening came on the now-empty streets...
strings.VEN_forpol.103.a: ...there would be nothing more to observe than silence.
strings.VEN_forpol.104.t: Fall of Venezuelan Government to Organisation of Free Nations Imminent
strings.VEN_forpol.104.desc:
TOP SECRET
EYES ONLY
TO ALL MEMBERS OF THE MINISTRY OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS

VENEZUELA - LATIN AMERICA

Venezuela is lost. Moncada Vidal's attempts to seize Essequibo and ensure the creation of a Guyanese satellite state were quickly repulsed by the garrison present and has quickly escalated into a full-scale conflict. Shore bombardments have commenced and the deteriorating security situation has resurrected Bolshevik elements within Venezuela. Civil war within the country seems both imminent and likely to be short-lived, a possibility that German elements in the country regularly warned him about.

At this stage, it is incredibly unlikely that Caracas will be able to reclaim lost ground, and will fall to Washington in a matter of weeks. Significant concessions are likely to be demanded beyond a recognition of Guyanese sovereignty in return for aid in quashing Bolshevik insurgency, and Venezuela will likely become an American puppet state. At this stage, little can be done beyond damage control. Place priority on removing personnel who moved to work in area and officially recognise Guyanese claim to Essequibo.
strings.VEN_forpol.104.a: All that money, thrown away for nothing?
strings.VEN_forpol.105.desc:
Troops move to the border. The factories are producing everything required as fast as they can. Material flows through the railroads and highways. Every possible preparation is being made for one of the most important moments in recent history.

We intend to make a stand against American imperialism, against their chokehold over the Americas. We ask you to aid us in that effort.

In 1887, we turned to America to aid us against the British, to make good upon their promises of being a new answer to the imperialists that took what they wanted without care. We asked them to mediate the Essequibo affair, even to be our representative, foolishly believing that they would stand up for us. They betrayed us, siding with the British while choosing influence and prestige over what was right. Even today, they use their OFN puppets to hold the land, a Canadian garrison just across our border, in order to maintain their ultimate control of the area after the British fell.

We now have the strength to rectify this mistake. The Americans and their chained thralls are strong, of that we have no delusion, but they are weak-willed. Their failure 30 years ago showed us that; the American public has no appetite for long wars that disturb their comfort. Meanwhile we possess the sense of will that only comes from righteousness. Our cause is just, and Venezuela's lands will no longer be held captive by foreign occupiers.

We ask you, as our closest ally, to aid us in this struggle. We can destroy the Canadians at the border and take our claims, but with you we can march all the way to Georgetown and send a message the whole world can hear. That the American beast can be beaten, their slaves can be pushed back, and that they need no longer fear the ugly American.
strings.VEN_forpol.105.a: A note from the Venezuelan ambassador, deposited discreetly at the highest desk.
strings.VEN_forpol.105.tt: Venezuela's ambitions over Essequibo will soon reach their climax...
strings.VEN_forpol.106.desc:
The campaign to reclaim Essequibo, the rightful Venezuelan territory under the occupation of Guiana, has begun. The troops and material that for so long has been collecting at the border, preparing for this very moment, have begun their operation and crashed into the unsuspecting Canadian garrison. No foreign force or Guyanese battalion shall be able to hold us; the success of our campaign is all but certain.

However, to complete our victory it is vital that we march forward together. The Americans have been slow to respond, but now their bluster and our intelligence has informed us that they are coming with their total superiority on sea and in the air. Troops shall pour into Georgetown and march to the border to attempt to hold us. The means of the American beast is infamous the world over, and we have no illusions as to its might. As such, we must ask you to aid us in this time of need - help us to strike a blow not just for Venezuela, not Latin America, but the whole world.

If we march forward, in-step with bayonets forward, the whole world can know that the age of American imperialism has ended, as America's humiliation shall be undeniable. We have shared with you our operational objectives in recent weeks, the operational plans have been made available to your officers. Now is the time to make use of that preparation, and help us liberate Essequibo.
strings.VEN_forpol.106.a: A discreet note, followed by an order to the generals. Aid would come to Venezuela.
strings.VEN_forpol.106.tt: You can now send volunteers to Venezuela.
strings.VEN_forpol.107.t: A Blow Heard Around the World
strings.VEN_forpol.107.desc:
Across the nation, fireworks shoot into the air. People chant in the streets and flags are raised; flags of Venezuela and flags of yours. Today, our victory has been achieved. Together we have liberated a region of Venezuela so long subjected to foreign enslavement, and we have struck a blow against the American monster upon our door.

The might of our combined efforts have rendered the OFN impotent, our forces standing strong even against their efforts to destroy us from afar. The American media already are turning upon their own nation like dogs, tearing at rancid meat. Questions over America's purpose, its ability to continue its empire faltering. Across Venezuela, we have speakers ensuring that our populace know this; this was no abortive coup nor FBI debacle. Venezuela fought the Americans and their thralls in open combat and came out the stronger.

But, as our speakers make clear in everything from radio broadcasts to television addresses, this achievement was not made alone.

Our government considers this an indication of the possibilities of continued cooperation, in light of our success driving back the imperialist clutches within Latin America. Collaboration offers an ever stronger future, one forged in the flames of liberation.
strings.VEN_forpol.107.a: For we made the world know that the strong must fear those they foolishly consider weak.
strings.VEN_forpol.108.desc:
We stood together, however our efforts to liberate Essequibo came to naught. Still it lingers under foreign occupation, our forces driven back to their starting positions by the might of the OFN-OAS response. From sea, air and land there was little chance to match the might of the American beast.

But, despite the unfortunate failure of the liberation we must not consider the operation a failure. Together we have bloodied the nose of the American giant, the corpses of their soldiers as well as those of their puppets will linger within their consciousness. We have made clear our position as a cornerstone of the resistance to the Empire, and wars are rarely won on their first battle.

What is clearer than ever is the importance of further collaboration. The might of America cannot be broken by a single nation, regardless of how committed they are to the cause of righteousness. America's military exists as a hammer more than adequate to squash the notion. Even now, the cowardly OAS continues to indulge American objectives, discussing the possibility of 'intervention' within our nation as if we were a mentally ill family member to be rectified. Should such discussions bear fruit, Venezuela may face a final crucible with the combined might of the OFN and OAS - if such an event, your aid will be essential. Only together can we continue to stand against the Americans, until the next opportunity for victory comes.
strings.VEN_forpol.108.a: The fire of defiance is dimming in Caracas.
